questions.q: WHO IS ELIGIBLE TO VOTE ABSENTEE?
questions.a: Any registered voter in Ohio.

questions.q: HOW DO I REQUEST AN ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a:
You can request an absentee ballot (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/VoterInformation.htm) and return the completed form through mail or in person.

You can request your absentee ballot for each election beginning on January 1st or 90 days before Election Day, whichever is earlier, but you must submit a separate absentee ballot application for each election in which you want to vote.

To request your absentee ballot, you must use the Secretary of State's official absentee ballot application form. Previously, applications were accepted in any form as long as all the required information was included, but the law has since changed.

questions.q: WHAT IS THE DEADLINE TO REQUEST AN ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a: The last day to request an absentee ballot (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/VoterInformation.htm) is 7 days before the election.

questions.q: WHAT IS THE DEADLINE FOR SUBMITTING AN ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a: Absentee ballots must be received by 7:30pm on Election Day.

questions.q: WHEN DOES ABSENTEE VOTING START?
questions.a:
Absentee voting begins 29 days before an election.

Once absentee ballots are available for voting, you may either vote in person at your county board of elections office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) or receive and return the absentee ballot via US mail or overnight delivery services, such as FedEx or UPS.

questions.q: HOW DO I GET MY ABSENTEE BALLOT AFTER I HAVE APPLIED?
questions.a:
When absentee voting begins, you can receive your absentee ballot either by mail or in person.

By mail: You must mail your completed absentee ballot application with your original signature to your county board of elections. (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) The board must receive your application 7 days before the election, but you should submit your request as far in advance of the election as possible to ensure you receive your absentee ballot before the election.

For more information, please contact the Ohio Secretary of State’s office (https://www.ohiosos.gov/elections/).

questions.q: CAN I TRACK MY MAILED ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a: You can sign up to track your absentee ballot (https://www.sos.state.oh.us/elections/voters/toolkit/ballot-tracking/) through the Ohio Secretary of State’s website.

questions.q: WHAT IF I REQUESTED AN ABSENTEE BALLOT BUT WANT TO VOTE IN PERSON?
questions.a:
If you requested an absentee ballot, you can still vote in person.

If you would like to vote at the county Early Vote Center you can during the Early Voting period (https://www.vote411.org/ohio#early-voting) and you can vote a regular ballot. If you would like to vote on Election Day you can, but you will have to vote a provisional ballot (https://www.vote411.org/ohio#provisional-voting). You will be asked for your absentee ballot during Early Voting, but if you do not have it with you, you can still vote on a regular ballot.

questions.q: HOW CAN I APPLY FOR AN ABSENTEE BALLOT IF I AM HOSPITALIZED ON ELECTION DAY?
questions.a:
If you are hospitalized on Election Day, regardless of where you are hospitalized, you must submit a properly completed and signed request to the board of elections of the county where your voting residence is located by 3:00 p.m. on Election Day.

To be eligible under this provision, you must be confined in a hospital because of an unforeseeable medical emergency, and your application must specify where, when, and why you came to be hospitalized.

You may include in your absentee ballot application a request that your county board of elections (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) give your unmarked ballot to a designated relative. A relative includes: your spouse, father, mother, father-in-law, mother-in-law, grandfather, grandmother, brother, sister, son, daughter, adopted parent, adopted child, stepparent, stepchild, uncle, aunt, nephew or niece. Your relative would then deliver the ballot to you in the hospital and return it to the board office after you have voted it.

If you are hospitalized in the same county where you are registered to vote, two representatives of the board of elections can deliver the ballot to you and return it to the board office.

questions.q: HOW DO I REQUEST AN ABSENTEE BALLOT AS AN OVERSEAS OR US MILITARY VOTER?
questions.a:
Overseas citizens and US military personnel can find information on how to register to vote and request an absentee ballot at the Overseas Vote Foundation. (https://www.overseasvotefoundation.org/vote/home.htm)

  Request your Ballot  (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/VoterInformation.htm)

questions.q: Does Ohio allow ballot curing?
questions.a: Yes, Ohio allows voters to fix an issue with their ballot.

questions.q: How will I know if there’s an issue with my absentee or mail-in ballot?
questions.a: If an error is found with your ballot, an election official will notify you of the issue by mail. The notice will include the necessary information and instructions to make the correction.

questions.q: What is the deadline to cure my ballot?
questions.a: The deadline to cure (correct) your absentee/mail ballot is the 4th day after the election.

questions.q: Can I track my absentee ballot?
questions.a: You can track your absentee ballot using your county’s online tool (https://www.sos.state.oh.us/elections/voters/toolkit/ballot-tracking/).

questions.q: How do I cure a provisional ballot?
questions.a: If you voted a provisional ballot, you have until the 4th day after the election to present evidence to support your eligibility to vote.

questions.q: What is a ballot drop box?
questions.a: A drop box is a secure, locked structure operated by election officials where voters can deliver their absentee ballot any time, day or night.

questions.q: Are drop boxes available in my state?
questions.a: Yes, vote-by-mail drop boxes are available in Ohio.

questions.q: Where can I find ballot drop box locations?
questions.a:
Each county in Ohio has one drop box that allows voters to return their Absentee Ballot Requests and Absentee Ballots at their Board of Elections in person.

Click here (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) to find the address of your Board of Elections.

Note: Only the voter can use outdoor drop boxes to return their voted absentee ballot. If a family member or someone assisting a voter with a disability needs to return it, they must bring it inside the election office and sign a form stating they’re allowed to under Ohio law.

questions.q: Can I track the ballot after placing in the drop box?
questions.a: Yes, you can track the status of your ballot request as well as your voted absentee ballot through the Voter Toolkit (https://www.ohiosos.gov/elections/voters/toolkit/).

questions.q: Can I vote before Election Day in Ohio?
questions.a: Yes. In Ohio, you can vote before Election Day by voting early in person or by voting by mail with an absentee ballot.

questions.q: Do I have to apply to vote early in Ohio?
questions.a: If you plan to vote early in person, no application is required. If you would like to vote before Election Day by mail, you must request an absentee ballot. No excuse is required.

questions.q: Where can I vote early in person in Ohio?
questions.a: You may vote early in person at your county’s early voting center. Find your early voting location here. (https://www.ohiosos.gov/directories/early-voting-locations)

questions.q: How can I receive an early ballot in the mail?
questions.a: Any registered voter in Ohio can vote by mail by requesting an absentee ballot. No excuse is required. Read more about requesting and returning your Absentee Ballot here. (https://www.vote411.org/ohio#absentee-ballot-process)

questions.q: Do I need an ID to vote early in Ohio?
questions.a: Yes. If you vote early in person, you must show an acceptable photo ID. If you vote by mail, you must provide identification information, such as your Ohio driver's license number, Ohio state ID number, or the last four digits of your Social Security number. Read more about voter ID requirements in Ohio here. (https://www.vote411.org/ohio#voter-id-requirements)

questions.q: Who is eligible to vote in Ohio?
questions.a:
To be eligible to vote you must be:

- A citizen of the United States
- At least 18 years old on or before the day of the general election
- A resident of Ohio for at least 30 days immediately before the election
- Not be incarcerated (in prison) for a felony conviction under the laws of the United States, this state or any other state of the United States
- Not been declared incompetent for voting purposes by a probate court
- You haven't been permanently disenfranchised for violating the election laws

questions.q: Can I vote in Ohio if I have a felony conviction?
questions.a: In Ohio, you only lose your right to vote if you are currently incarcerated for a felony conviction. If you lost your voting rights because of a conviction, you could register to vote immediately after release. Your voting rights are not restricted by pretrial detention, misdemeanors, probation, or parole.

questions.q: How do I vote in Ohio if I don’t have a permanent address?
questions.a: You can register and vote in Ohio even if you do not have a traditional home address. You must provide a location that describes where you live, such as a shelter, park, or street intersection, and a mailing address where you can receive election information.

questions.q: Can students vote in Ohio?
questions.a: Yes. Students may register and vote in Ohio if they meet the state's voter eligibility requirements. Students can choose to register at their school address or their home address, but they may only be registered and vote in one location.

questions.q: Do I need an ID to register to vote in Ohio?
questions.a: It depends on how you register. If you register online you will need to provide the below ID.

questions.q: What types of ID are accepted for registration?
questions.a:
If you register online, you will need to provide the following:

- Ohio driver’s license or Ohio identification card number
- Name
- Date of Birth
- Address
- Last four digits of your Social Security number

questions.q: What if I don’t have an ID?
questions.a:
If you do not have any portion of the required information, follow this link to update your voting address using our paper form (PDF). (https://www.ohiosos.gov/globalassets/elections/forms/vr_form_04-2015.pdf) Once you complete this form, you must sign and send it to your county board of elections (https://www.ohiosos.gov/elections/elections-officials/county-boards-of-elections-directory/). (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm)

If you are a Safe at Home participant, before you proceed, please follow this link to contact the Safe at Home office (https://www.ohiosos.gov/secretary-office/office-initiatives/safe-at-home/victims/).

Voters can call or text 844-338-8743 at any time to reach VoteRiders Voter ID Helpline

questions.q: When are official election results available in Ohio?
questions.a: Official results are never available on Election Day. Election officials are working around the clock to count a large number of ballots, and it’s essential that they take the time to make sure every vote is counted.

questions.q: Where can I find official election results?
questions.a:
Official election results will be uploaded on Ohio’s Secretary of State website (https://www.sos.state.oh.us/elections/election-results-and-data/) as they become available.

  Official Results  (https://www.sos.state.oh.us/elections/election-results-and-data/)

questions.q: What does a poll worker do in Ohio?
questions.a: Poll workers generally help run elections by setting up polling locations, checking in voters, issuing ballots, assisting voters, operating voting equipment, and helping open and close the polls.

questions.q: What qualifications do I need to be a poll worker in Ohio?
questions.a:
In order to be a poll worker in Ohio, you must:

- Be a U.S. citizen
- Be at least 18 years of age and registered to vote or 17 years old and in high school
- Be a resident of the county in which you plan to serve
- Not be a candidate on the ballot in the precinct you are working
- Have not been convicted of a felony

All poll workers are required to attend a training session scheduled by their county board of elections prior to the election.

questions.q: Are poll workers paid in Ohio?
questions.a: Yes. Poll workers are paid for their service, and some counties also provide paid training. Compensation varies by county and position. Contact your county board of elections (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for specific pay information.

questions.q: How do I apply to be a poll worker in Ohio?
questions.a: Sign up online (https://www.ohiosos.gov/elections/poll-worker-recruitment/sign-up-to-be-a-poll-worker) through your state's poll worker application or contact your county board of elections (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) to apply.

questions.q: What is a provisional ballot?
questions.a: Provisional ballots ensure that all voters can cast a ballot even if voter eligibility isn’t certain when they vote. Voters can mark a provisional ballot, and election workers set it aside until eligibility is verified at a later time.

questions.q: Does Ohio offer provisional voting?
questions.a: Yes, Ohio offers provisional voting.

questions.q: What are some reasons to vote a provisional ballot?
questions.a:
There are several scenarios where a voter may cast a provisional ballot:

- Your name does not appear on the official poll list for the precinct or an election official asserts that you are not eligible to vote or is unable to determine your eligibility
- You are unable or decline to provide the required proof of identity
- Your name appears on the official poll list for that precinct as having already requested an absentee ballot
- Your name is marked on the poll list or signature book with a notation that certain registration mailings have been returned as undeliverable.
- A hearing on a challenge to your eligibility as an elector has been postponed until after Election Day.
- In the opinion of the precinct officers, your signature does not match the signature on your registration form.
- Your eligibility to cast a ballot has been challenged by the precinct officials.

questions.q: How do I cure a provisional ballot?
questions.a:
Before your provisional ballot can be included in the official count of an election, the board of elections must confirm your eligibility to cast the ballot and the validity of the ballot you cast. If you cast a provisional ballot and provided acceptable proof of identity, you typically do not need to provide any additional information.

If you cast a provisional ballot and did not provide acceptable proof of identity at the time of voting, you must appear in person at the Board of Elections no later than seven days following the election to provide such proof within the 4 days immediately following Election Day.

Acceptable proof of identity includes:

- Current and valid photo ID
- A military identification
- The last four digits of your Social Security number

questions.q: When are provisional ballots counted?
questions.a: Provisional ballots are counted until the 8th day after Election Day or until any hearing required under State Law with regard to the provisional voter is held, whichever is earlier. The counting of absentee ballots begins on the 5th day following an election.

questions.q: What voting assistance is available for voters with disabilities?
questions.a:
The Help America Vote Act requires that election authorities have voting equipment for voters with disabilities to vote privately and independently, and Ohio is no exception.

Polling places should provide touch screen voting machines and have audio adaptations for assisting the blind.

There are also adaptations for voters with lack of muscle control.

If you have a disability, you may also have assistance by two election officials (of different political parties) or by the person of your choice (except employer or union agent).

If the polling place is not accessible for you, you may vote a ballot from your vehicle at all polling places.

For more information on the provisions available for disabled voters, please contact your local election authority (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: How do I request accommodation or report accessibility issues?
questions.a: If you have any questions about receiving help in voting, please ask the clerk or inspector at the polling place.

questions.q: Can I vote by mail because of my disability?
questions.a:
Vote-by-mail (absentee voting) is available in Ohio and no excuse is required. You can find more about how to vote by mail here. (https://www.vote411.org/ohio#absentee-ballot-process)

For more information, you can utilize the American Association of People With Disabilities (AAPD) (http://www.aapd.com/what-we-do/voting/) resource.

questions.q: Does Ohio require employers to give time off to vote?
questions.a: Yes. Ohio employers must provide employees a reasonable amount of time off to vote on Election Day. Talk to your employer and make a plan to vote ahead of Election Day.

questions.q: Do I need an ID to vote in Ohio?
questions.a: Yes. Ohio voters must provide identification when voting, whether voting in person or by absentee ballot.

questions.q: What types of ID can I use to vote in-person in Ohio?
questions.a:
You can use one of the following unexpired photo IDs to vote in Ohio:

- Ohio driver's license
- Ohio state ID card
- Interim ID form issued by the Ohio Bureau of Motor Vehicles
- U.S. passport or passport card
- U.S. military ID card
- Ohio National Guard ID card
- U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs ID card

The name on your ID must substantially conform to your name in the poll book.

questions.q: What types of ID can I use to vote absentee in Ohio?
questions.a:
When voting by mail, you must provide one of the following on your absentee ballot application and identification envelope:

- Ohio driver's license number
- Ohio state ID number
- The last four digits of your Social Security number

questions.q: What if I don’t have an acceptable ID?
questions.a: If you do not have an acceptable photo ID, you can vote using a provisional ballot (https://www.vote411.org/ohio#provisional-voting). To have your ballot counted, you must provide an acceptable form of identification to your county board of elections within four days after Election Day. You may also obtain a free Ohio state ID card from the Bureau of Motor Vehicles (https://www.bmv.ohio.gov/dl-id-card.aspx).

questions.q: Can I use my student ID to vote in Ohio?
questions.a:
No. Student IDs are not accepted as voter identification in Ohio.

Voters can call or text 844-338-8743 at any time to reach VoteRiders Voter ID Helpline

questions.q: What is the deadline to register to vote in Ohio?
questions.a:
- Online registration deadline: 30 days before Election Day
- Register by mail deadline: Postmarked 30 days before Election Day
- In-person registration deadline: 30 days before Election Day

questions.q: How can I register to vote in Ohio?
questions.a:
- Register online (https://www.vote411.org/register)
- By mail: Send your completed and signed registration form (https://www.ohiosos.gov/elections/elections-administration/forms-and-petitions/voter-registration-form-html-to-pdf) to your county board of elections or the Secretary of State’s office. You may also request that a form be mailed to you.
- Register in person at the DMV (Department of Motor Vehicles)
- Register in person at:
- The Ohio Secretary of State’s office
- Any of Ohio’s 88 county boards of elections
- Any Bureau of Motor Vehicles (BMV) registrar or deputy registrar office
- Public libraries, high schools, vocational schools, or county treasurers’ offices

questions.q: What do I need to register online?
questions.a:
To register online you will need to provide the following:

- Name
- Date of Birth
- Address
- Ohio driver’s license or Ohio identification card number
- Last four digits of your Social Security number

 If you are missing any of the required information listed above, follow this link to update your voting address using the paper form (PDF). (https://www.ohiosos.gov/globalassets/elections/forms/vr_form_04-2015.pdf) Once you complete this form, you must sign and send it to your county board of elections (https://www.ohiosos.gov/elections/elections-officials/county-boards-of-elections-directory/).

questions.q: How can I check my voter registration status?
questions.a: You can verify your voter registration status using Ohio’s voter information tool. (https://voterlookup.ohiosos.gov/voterlookup.aspx)

questions.q: Does Ohio have online voter registration?
questions.a: Yes! Use our online registration tool (https://www.vote411.org/register) to complete your application

questions.q: Is same-day voter registration available in Ohio?
questions.a: No, Ohio does not have same-day voter registration.

questions.q: Can I pre-register to vote?
questions.a: Yes, you can pre-register at age 17 if you’ll be 18 years old on or before the next general election.

questions.q: Who is eligible to register in Ohio?
questions.a: Check if you’re eligible to register here (https://www.vote411.org/ohio#eligibility-requirements).

questions.q: What types of voting machines does Ohio use?
questions.a: The voting systems used in Minnesota are Optical Scan and Direct Recording Electronic (DRE).

questions.q: What is optical scan voting?
questions.a:
With optical scan voting, you will receive a card or sheet of paper, which you take over to a private table or booth. The card has the names of the various candidates and ballot measures printed on it.

- With a pen or pencil, you fill in a little box, circle, or space between two arrows.
- When you are finished filling out all the cards, you may bring the cards over to a ballot box, where poll workers will show you how to put the cards in the box.
- Or in some places, you may feed the completed cards or papers into a computer device that checks your card or paper right there at the polling place to make sure you have voted the way you want to and counts the votes.

questions.q: What is Direct Recording Electronic Voting?
questions.a:
Direct Recording Electronic (DRE) is the newest system in use in the U.S. All the information about who and what you are voting for is on an electronic screen like a TV or computer screen.

There are many variations of DREs because many companies are inventing new ones, and many cities, counties, and states are trying them out.

- Usually, after you have signed in, the poll workers will give you a card that you slide into a device to start your voting session.
- Some of these devices will show all candidates and ballot choices on one big screen. Often, with these big screen devices you push a button next to the name of the candidate you want to vote for (or yes or no on a ballot measure).
- On other DREs, the screen is set up to show pages. There will probably be one thing on which to vote on each screen or page. For example, on one screen or page, you might vote for the president. Then you might move to the next page to vote for a senator. Often these small-screen devices have a touch screen, where you touch the screen next to the name of the person you want to vote for.
- Other devices have a keypad, and some have a keyboard, so you can write in the name of someone you want to vote for.
- You let the system know you are finished voting by pushing a button, touching the screen or entering something on a keypad.

You can learn more about voting systems by checking out the Elections Assistance Commission's (EAC) resource.  (https://www.eac.gov/voting-equipment/system-certification-process)
